author: Miguel de Cervantes

The book is a scan with no text layer, so this file is the record of that reading and is what every question is checked against. These are notes on the action, not the book's text. Page 63 opens in mid-sentence: the chain gang first comes into view on page 62, which is not part of tonight's reading.

facts: The page opens mid-sentence on the party coming along the road: men on horseback with muskets, and two men on foot carrying pikes and swords
As soon as Sancho saw them he said it was a chain gang, impressed by the king and going to the galleys
Don Quixote asked what impressed meant, and whether the king really has the power to impress anyone he pleases
Sancho explained that those men had been condemned by the king for their crimes to serve in the galleys, and were being taken there by force
Don Quixote concluded that they were not going of their own free will, and Sancho agreed that this was true
Don Quixote said that this was an occasion for him to perform his duty, which is to oppose violence and help those who are suffering
Sancho argued back that the king does no wrong or violence to such men for the sake of justice, but only punishes them for their crimes
By this time the chain gang had come up to them
Don Quixote used many courteous phrases to the guards and asked why the men were being conducted along in chains

glossary.galleys: Low ships moved by oars and sails that were often used in war.

facts: One mounted guard replied that the men were convicts, the slaves of the King, going to the galleys, and that there was no more to be said about it
The other mounted guard, who acted as chief, said they carried the official records of the wretches, but that it was not a convenient time to read them out
Don Quixote said that all the same he would like to learn from each man individually the cause of his misfortune
The first man answered that he was there for falling in love
Don Quixote exclaimed that if a man is sent to the galleys for that, he himself should be rowing there
The fellow explained that his was not that sort of love: his affection had been for a laundry basket of fine linen, and only the force of the law separated him from it
He had been caught in the act, so nobody needed to torture him into confessing
His sentence was a hundred lashes across the shoulders and three years in the galleys
Don Quixote asked the second man the same question, but the man was too sad to answer, so the first convict answered on his behalf
The first convict said the second man passed for a canary, which is to say a singer
Don Quixote asked whether singers really are sent to the galleys
A full-page engraving of Don Quixote on Rocinante, lance in hand, facing the chained convicts and their mounted guards
The caption beneath repeats his line from page 64, that he would like to learn from each of them the cause of his misfortune
There is no story text on this page
The convict said there is nothing worse than singing while you are in pain
Don Quixote replied with the saying that to sing in grief gives relief
The convict said it is the opposite here, because a man who sings once may weep for the rest of his life
Don Quixote said he did not understand
A guard explained that among these rogues, singing in pain means confessing under torture
The guard said this man had been tortured and had confessed to stealing cattle
His sentence was six years in the galleys plus two hundred lashes on the shoulders
The guard said the man is always downcast because the other convicts hate and abuse him for confessing, since he had not the nerve to go on denying his guilt
The convicts say among themselves that No is as easy to say as Yes
The guard said they reckon a criminal has good luck when his fate depends only on his own tongue rather than on witnesses and evidence, and that he thought they were mostly right
Don Quixote moved on to the third convict
This man told his story freely and carelessly, saying he was going to the galleys for want of ten ducats
Don Quixote offered him twenty ducats to relieve him of his situation
The convict answered that if he had had those twenty ducats at the right moment he could have paid a lawyer

The third convict finished his point: with a smooth-talking lawyer he would be standing free today in the marketplace of Toledo instead of travelling this road on a leash, but God is great and he must be patient
Don Quixote moved on to the fourth man, who had a long gray beard hanging down on his chest
The fourth man wept and said not a word
The man beside him explained that this fellow was going to the galleys for four years for selling women to men, witchcraft and fortune-telling
The old man admitted the offenses but said he had meant no harm, and lamented that at his age and in his state of health he would never be free again
Sancho felt such compassion for the old man that he took a coin from his own pocket and gave it to him in charity
Don Quixote moved on to the next man, who described his tangled relations with girls with more liveliness than any of the others
That man said the proofs were clear against him, and that having no friends and no money, and his neck about to be stretched, he was satisfied with the price of six years in the galleys
He added that he was still young, and while there is life there is hope
This man wore the clothes of a student, and one of the guards said he was a wonderful speaker
Last of all came a fine-looking cross-eyed man of about thirty, chained hand and foot
The last man wore an extra iron collar around his neck, and his hands were manacled to an iron belt at his waist so that he could not raise them to his head or lower his head to reach them
Don Quixote asked why this man was so specially guarded
An officer answered that he was guilty of more crimes than all the rest put together, and was so desperate and violent a ruffian that despite his shackles they always feared he would escape
Don Quixote asked what crimes could deserve no more punishment than being sent to the galleys
The guard answered that the man was going for ten years, which is like being condemned to death
The guard named him as Gines de Pasamonte, also called Ginesillo de Parapilla
The guard said Gines had written a clever history of his own life and had left the book in pawn at the prison for two hundred reals
Don Quixote asked whether the book was finished
Gines answered for himself that he could not finish it while he was still alive
Gines said that so far it told everything about him, from his birth up to this latest sentence to the galleys
Don Quixote asked whether he had been sent before
Gines replied that he had already done four years in the service of God and his country, that he knew the taste of ship's biscuit and of the lash, and that he was not much troubled about going again
Gines said he was not troubled about going back because he would have time to write and had many more things to say, and that the galleys of Spain give a man leisure enough for that purpose
Don Quixote told him he seemed clever
Gines answered that he was also unfortunate, because misfortune always persecutes genius
The chief guard said that it persecutes rascals, rather
Gines said that was enough, and that they should get on
At this Don Quixote turned around to the chain gang and addressed them all

He said that from everything they had told him he gathered that, although they were being punished for their crimes, what they were going through was not to their taste and they were not going to the galleys of their own good will

He said their condemnation might have been caused by one man's lack of endurance under torture, another's lack of money, another's lack of influential friends, and the prejudiced views of their judges, and that they had not had the full justice they were entitled to
He said all this was urging him, even forcing him, to make clear through them why Heaven had sent him into the world to be a professor of chivalry
He said he had sworn to help the wretched and to defend those who are oppressed by the strong
He said that what can be done by fair means should not be done by force
He therefore began to beg the gentlemen who were guarding them
Don Quixote finished his request: he begged the guards to free the men and let them depart in peace
He said many others would serve the king with a better will, and that it seemed to him a hard case to make slaves of those whom God and nature had made free
He told the guards that these poor fellows had done them no wrong, that we are all offenders here on earth, and that there is a God above who will punish the bad and reward the good
He said it was a reasonable request, made meekly and gently so that he could thank them for granting it, but that if they refused, his lance and sword and invincible arm would force them to
The chief guard called this pleasant foolery, and said the silly mouse had popped his head out of his hole at last
The chief guard said Don Quixote wanted them to release the prisoners of the king, as though the guards had the authority to do it or he had the power to command it
The chief guard told him to go on his way in peace, to mind the barber's bowl he wore on his head, and not to go looking for five legs on a cat
Don Quixote answered that the guard was a mouse and a cat himself
He immediately attacked the officer, who had no chance to defend himself, and drove him to the ground with a lance thrust that wounded him badly
For a moment the other guards were stunned by the unexpected attack, but they soon advanced on Don Quixote, who calmly waited for them
